Cycloidal actuators.

When the first reducer would not back-drive

My early cycloidal actuator wasn’t back-drivable, and its mechanical losses limited the joint response I wanted.

The reducer assembled and turned under motor power, but resistance in the mechanism was still a problem. I began looking more closely at how the output shaft carried the load and how much clearance the gear profile needed.

Disk geometry and bearing support

I parameterized the cycloidal disk and pin geometry in SolidWorks, then worked through eccentricity, shaft and bearing support, output interfaces, and the housing. Printing and assembling prototypes showed where fits needed revision.

Speed, torque, and efficiency
ωout = ωmotor / G
τout ≈ ηGτmotor
η = Pout / Pin

G is the reduction ratio, and η is the efficiency at a stated operating point. Back-driving resistance needs its own test.

What I changed

  1. Mechanical improvement

    Redesign the output-shaft structure and refine gear-profile clearance

    Improving the output-shaft structure and adjusting gear-profile clearance made the actuator more efficient and easier to back-drive. I carried those changes into later prototypes while continuing to refine the fits and assembly.

  2. Packaging revisions

    Make room for the electronics and the assembly process

    The package had to accommodate the controller board, bearings, output flange, and motor. Our project review also identified heat near printed parts, airflow, wiring routes, and fastener access as areas for further work.

  3. Documented reducer variants

    Compare the 17:1 and 25:1 designs

    The repository retains the original 17:1 design, which is no longer maintained, alongside the revised 25:1 assembly. The newer version uses a different output-shaft sleeve bearing and addresses torque margin. The output-shaft and clearance revisions addressed the mechanical losses.

Reduction also changes reflected inertia
Jmotor → output = G²Jmotor
Jload → motor = Jload / G²

These ideal relations describe how reduction affects the inertia seen at each side of the actuator. I consider that effect alongside torque margin and back-driving resistance.

Measuring the prototypes

I developed a dynamometer layout and fixture tests to examine torque, efficiency, backlash, repeatability, and temperature rise. For a fair comparison between revisions, speed, load, warm-up state, and measurement method need to match.

The output-shaft and gear-clearance revisions improved the mechanism, but I haven’t assigned them a calibrated before-and-after efficiency or back-drive torque rating.

What I’m exploring next

PROJECT STATUS

Printed prototypes integrated into the robot.

We integrated the cycloidal prototypes into the robot. I’m now exploring lower reduction and a different motor package through the planetary QDD study, which is at the CAD stage.
